title: Former Eminem Employee Pleads Guilty to Criminal Infringement of Copyright
body: Press Release Former Eminem Employee Pleads Guilty to Criminal Infringement of Copyright Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Michigan DETROIT — Joseph Strange, 48, of Holly, Michigan, who was formerly employed by the artist and musician Marshall Mathers (also known as Eminem), pleaded guilty in the Eastern District of Michigan to a charge related to his role in the reproduction and sale of unreleased music created by Eminem. “Our republic is built on the right to property,” said U.S. Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon Jr. for the Eastern District of Michigan. “We will protect that right by punishing criminals who steal the physical or intellectual property of Americans.” “Joseph Strange abused a position of trust to unlawfully copy and sell unreleased music belonging to Eminem, profiting from works that were not yet authorized for public distribution,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “His conduct undermined both legal and artistic rights. The Criminal Division remains committed to protecting intellectual property, holding accountable those who seek to profit from theft of creative content, and working with our law enforcement partners to deter and disrupt these crimes.” “Detroit has always been a city where creativity thrives, and no one has the right to steal or profit from another artist’s work without their permission,” said Special Agent in Charge Jennifer Runyan of the FBI Detroit Field Office. “Today’s guilty plea reinforces a simple principle: accountability follows those who compromise the integrity of another person’s creative labor. I want to commend the outstanding work of our FBI Oakland County Resident Agency and the entire investigative team, whose persistence and professionalism drove this case forward. We also appreciate the cooperation of Mathers Music Studio throughout the investigation. Protecting intellectual property means protecting the time, talent, and livelihoods behind it, and we will continue to treat these violations with the seriousness they deserve.” According to court documents, Strange was an employee of Mathers from approximately 2007 until 2021. During Strange’s employment, he worked at a studio in Ferndale, Michigan that Mathers used to create and develop music for future sale and distribution. During his employment, Strange helped set up and operate a computer system that stored music created by Mathers. Strange had access to password-protected hard drives that contained music in the process of being developed by Mathers and that was not yet meant to be released to the public. At some point Strange — without authority — copied 10 or more audio files of music and material in various stages of development from one or more of these drives. Between July and August of 2024, Strange sold and transmitted 10 or more of these music files to purchasers via the internet for a total of approximately $50,000. Strange did so without Mathers’s knowledge or authorization. Audio files sold by Strange were ultimately released online and made available on various public streaming platforms, without the permission or prior knowledge of Mathers. According to facts alleged by the government, while no commercial release of the music or material within these files was imminent or even certain, professional efforts had been made to prepare some of the music for possible commercial release, in some cases including studio mastering. Data provided by several streaming providers evidenced that, as of November 2025, infringing audio files identified by the government had been accessed more than eight million times. The infringement amount of the stolen files is estimated to be at least $750,000. Strange pleaded guilty to criminal infringement of a copyright. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 27, 2027, and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The FBI is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Timothy Wyse and Alyse Wu for the Eastern District of Michigan and Senior Counsel Vasantha Rao of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS) are prosecuting the case. CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds. Updated October 22, 2026 Topic Intellectual Property Component USAO - Michigan, Eastern

title: Federal Jury Convicts Monahans Man of Three Counts After He Sexually Abused a Child for Over Five Years
body: Press Release Federal Jury Convicts Monahans Man of Three Counts After He Sexually Abused a Child for Over Five Years Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Texas ALPINE, Texas – A federal jury in Pecos convicted a Monahans man for two counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child under 12 and one count of committing a sexual offense while being required to register as a sex offender, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Michael Scott Nichols, 55, groomed and sexually abused a minor female from around the age of six years old until she was 11 years old. On Sept. 23, 2024, the Ward County Sheriff's Department responded to a home in Monahans, where a woman reported that her daughter had been molested by Nichols. Nichols is a registered sex offender due to convictions for sexual assault of a child in 1995 and in 1997. He was sentenced to 15 years in a Texas State Prison for the 1997 offense. During this investigation, it was discovered that Nichols, who owned a trucking company, had abused the minor victim in the Western District of Texas and also transported her across state lines and further abused the victim in other states. Nichols was arrested on April 15, 2025. A third superseding indictment filed in August 2026 charged him with two counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child and one count of penalties for registered sex offenders. A federal jury found Nichols guilty on all three counts on Wednesday, concluding a three-day trial held before U.S. District Judge David Counts. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations and the Ward County Sheriff's Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kevin Cayton and Heather Haywood are prosecuting the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC . ### Contact USATXW.MediaInquiry@usdoj.gov Updated October 22, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Texas, Western

title: New Orleans Couple Indicted for Violations of the Federal Controlled Substances Act and Federal Gun Control Act
body: Press Release New Orleans Couple Indicted for Violations of the Federal Controlled Substances Act and Federal Gun Control Act Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS, LA – On October 15, 2026, ALFRED FLANAGIN (“FLANAGIN”), age 42, and ASHA GANPAT (“ GANPAT” ), age 46, of New Orleans, were indicted for conspiracy to distribute, and possess with intent to distribute, controlled substances and use of a communication facility in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(B), 841(b)(1)(C), 841(b)(1)(D), 841(b)(1)(E), 843(b), and 846, announced United States Attorney David I. Courcelle. FLANAGIN was also indicted for possession with intent to distribute controlled substances, possession of firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and maintaining a drug-involved premises, in violation of Title 21, United States Code Sections 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(B), 841(b)(1)(C), 841(b)(1)(D), 841(b)(1)(E), and 856(a)(2), and Title 18, United States Code, Section 924(c)(1)(A). According to court records, on October 2, 2026, FLANAGIN allegedly possessed with intent to distribute fifty grams or more of a mixture and substance containing methamphetamine, a quantity of a mixture and substance containing ketamine, a quantity of a mixture and substance containing ecstasy, and a quantity of marijuana. FLANAGIN is also alleged to have used and maintained a drug-involved premises on Louisiana Avenue Parkway in New Orleans, and possessed four firearms and numerous amounts of ammunition in furtherance of his drug trafficking activities. GANPAT is alleged to have conspired with FLANAGIN to distribute narcotics in the New Orleans area and used a communications device in furtherance of same. If convicted of conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances, FLANAGIN and GANPAT face a minimum of five (5) up to forty (40) years of imprisonment, up to a $5,000,000 fine, and at least four (4) years of supervised release. If convicted of possession with intent to distribute controlled substances, FLANAGIN faces a minimum term of five (5) years up to a maximum term of forty (40) years imprisonment, a fine of up to $5,000,000, and at least four (4) years of supervised release. If convicted of possessing firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, FLANAGIN faces a minimum consecutive sentence of five (5) years up to life of imprisonment, up to a $250,000 fine, and up to 5 years of supervised release. If convicted of maintaining a drug-involved premises, FLANAGIN faces up to twenty (20) years of imprisonment, up to a $500,000 fine, and at least 3 years of supervised release. FLANAGIN and GANPAT also face payment of a $100 mandatory special assessment fee for each charged offense. U.S. Attorney Courcelle reiterated that the indictment is merely a charge and that the guilt of the defendants must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The case was investigated by the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, Homeland Security Investigation, and the New Orleans Police Department. It is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Mary Ellen Buntin of the Narcotics Unit. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. *        *        * Contact Shane M. title: St. Louis County Man Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Attempting Sexual Contact with Jefferson County Teen
body: Press Release St. Louis County Man Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Attempting Sexual Contact with Jefferson County Teen Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Missouri ST. LOUIS – U.S. District Judge Cristian M. Stevens on Thursday sentenced a St. Louis County man to 10 years in prison for trying to have sexual contact with a Jefferson County 14-year-old. Judge Stevens also placed Tay’vion K. Like, 25, on supervised release for life after his release from prison, saying he was concerned about a prior conviction for indecent exposure and needed to protect children in the community. Judge Stevens also ordered Like to pay restitution to the victim of $1,210. In July of 2025, Like was communicating with the teen via Snapchat. He asked for sexual contact with the victim, even after she told him that she was 14. Like claimed he was 17. Like then told her that he wanted to come to her house to engage in sexual activity. She told him not to come, and that she would call police. When she discovered that he was outside her house on July 15, 2025, she tried to get him to leave and then told her father. Her father called the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies caught Like near the victim’s home. Like also admitted communicating in a sexual manner with other underage girls on Snapchat. Like, of Bellefontaine Neighbors, pleaded guilty in July in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of coercion and enticement of a minor. The Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office and the FBI investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jillian Anderson prosecuted the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Department of Justice Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc . Contact Robert Patrick, Public Affairs Officer, robert.patrick@usdoj.gov. title: Beaverton Man Sentenced to Two Years and Nine Months in Federal Prison for Possession with Intent to Distribute Fentanyl
body: Press Release Beaverton Man Sentenced to Two Years and Nine Months in Federal Prison for Possession with Intent to Distribute Fentanyl Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon PORTLAND, Ore.— U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon Scott Bradford announced today that Eder Fletes Calix , 24, of Beaverton, Oregon, was sentenced to two years and nine months in federal prison, to be followed by five years of supervised release, for possessing more than 700 grams of fentanyl with intent to distribute. The sentence follows a multi-agency investigation that began in March 2025, when an Oregon State Trooper conducted a traffic stop on a vehicle driven by Fletes Calix. During the encounter, the trooper observed drug paraphernalia and cash in the vehicle. Both Fletes Calix and a co-defendant fled the scene on foot, prompting the execution of a search warrant that revealed more than 400 grams of compressed fentanyl powder inside the vehicle. Over the following months, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) continued the investigation and observed multiple drug transactions involving Fletes Calix and his co-defendant. Agents seized additional quantities of fentanyl from buyers during two separate stops in May and June 2025. On July 2, 2025, federal agents arrested Fletes Calix and executed multiple search warrants, including at a Beaverton residence where he had been renting a room. Agents recovered approximately $22,000 in cash, drug packaging materials, digital scales, and additional quantities of fentanyl. In total, investigators seized approximately 767.9 grams of fentanyl powder from the defendants’ vehicle, residence, and related transactions. During a post-arrest interview, Fletes Calix admitted he knew the substance was fentanyl and acknowledged that he and his co-defendant were selling it. Fletes Calix pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl, a Schedule II controlled substance. In determining the sentence, the Court considered the severity of the offense, the volume of fentanyl involved, and Fletes Calix’s lack of criminal history. The case was investigated by the DEA and the Oregon State Police. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jessica Keefer and Kate Rochat. Velderrain Perez No. 26-MJ-05136 (Southern District of California) AUSA Emily Allen On September 2, 2026, prosecutors charged Juan Velderrain Perez with smuggling 24 one-liter bottles of Taktic pesticide into the United States (18 U.S.C. § 545). On August 19, 2026, Velderrain Perez attempted to cross the border at the Otay Mesa Port of Entry with the illegal pesticides concealed in his car. The defendant admitted that he had entered the U.S. with illegal pesticides before. Taktic contains the active ingredient amitraz at a concentration banned in the U.S. by the Environmental Protection Agency since 2019. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division and Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation. Related Press Release: https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdca/pr/mexican-man-charged-smuggling-banned-pesticides United States v. Lonnie S. Gaskins, et al . No. 4:26-CR-00769 (District of South Carolina) AUSA Elle Klein AUSA Holly Brown On September 3, 2026, the court arraigned Lonnie Shane Gaskins, Terry James Gaskins, Shamar O'Ryan Sutton, Avery Robinson, Derwayne Terry Miller, Sr., and Kevin Knotts on charges of conspiracy to violate the Animal Welfare Act and possessing dogs for use in animal fighting ventures (7 U.S.C. § 2156(b) and 18 U.S.C. § 49(a); 18 U.S.C. § 371). Terry James Gaskins and Miller were also charged with unlawful possession of firearms (18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1), 924(a)(8)). Between September 2019 and July 2026, the defendants bred, housed, and trained pit bull-type dogs for dog fighting. They used equipment and paraphernalia to train the dogs, including treadmills, bite sticks, and heavy metal chains. They shared images and videos of  fighting and injured dogs and exchanged texts discussing the training and fighting of dogs. Between April and July 2026, law enforcement executed five search warrants at the defendants’ residences, seizing a total of 100 dogs along with dog fighting paraphernalia. The U.S. Department of Agriculture Office of the Inspector General, South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, Homeland Security Investigations, and the U.S. Marshal Service conducted the investigation. Photo of dog filed with government bond pleading Related Press Release: District of South Carolina | Dog Fighting Investigation Results in Largest Single Property Dog Seizure in South Carolina History, 7 Men Charged | United States Department of Justice United States v. Taurean Jaquan Servance, et al. No. 1:26-CR-00027 (Northern District of Florida) AUSA Adam M. Hapner On September 15, 2026, a court finished arraigning the last of six defendants on the indictment charging them with conspiracy and engaging in an animal fighting venture (18 U.S.C. § 49, 7 U.S.C. § 2156(a)(1)). (The indicted defendants are Taurean Jaquan Servance, Jarrett Abram Servance, Jarrett Abram Servance, Jr., Terry Lajace Lee, Christopher Eugene Thompson, and Clinton Thomas. Trial is scheduled to begin on October 21, 2026. Between April 2022 and October 2025, the defendants bred, housed, and trained pit bull-type dogs for dog fighting. They used equipment to train the dogs, including treadmills, bite sticks, and heavy metal chains. They also shared images and videos of the dogs, as well as texts discussing training and fighting dogs. Local law enforcement officials seized 42 dogs. The U.S. Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General, the Gainesville Police Department, Alachua County Sherriff’s Office, and Alachua County Animal Resources conducted the investigation. Related Press Release: Northern District of Florida | Six Gainesville Men Indicted for Dog Fighting Offenses | United States Department of Justice Guilty Pleas United States v. Yenkin Majestic Paint Corporation No. 2:26-CR-00093 (Southern District of Ohio) ECS Senior Trial Attorney Adam Cullman AUSA David Twombly ECS Paralegal Jillian Grubb On September 1, 2026, Yenkin Majestic Paint Corporation (Yenkin) pleaded guilty to violating the negligent endangerment provision of the Clean Air Act for an explosion that killed one employee and injured many more (42 U.S.C. § 7413(c)(4)). Yenkin manufactured industrial coatings and resin in Columbus, Ohio. The manufacturing process involved heating ingredients in large steel vessels known as “kettles.” In 2020, Yenkin fabricated and installed a new door, known as a “manway,” on top of Kettle 3. This door allowed access inside the kettle. Yenkin completed installation of the new manway in December 2020 . Despite several high-pressure spikes, Yenkin never pressure tested the new manway before placing Kettle 3 back in service. The door began leaking immediately after installation. Yenkin chose not to take Kettle 3 out of service, opting instead to add a thicker gasket that the company mistakenly thought was made of Teflon, but was actually silicone. On April 8, 2021, Yenkin employees were producing resin in Kettle 3. The operator did not know that the agitator had stopped, likely due to electrical work Yenkin was conducting at the time. When the operator switched the agitator back on, it caused the contents to vaporize and increase the pressure inside the kettle. Moments later, the manway and gasket could no longer contain the pressure and began releasing a mixture of hot resin liquid and flammable solvent vapor into the plant. Multiple flammable gas detectors inside the facility started detecting an increase in the concentration of flammable vapors during the release. However, the flammable gas detectors were not configured to sound an audible alarm. At 12:04 a.m., the released flammable vapors found an ignition source and exploded, which led to the death of one employee and severe injuries to several others. The explosion also damaged the resin plant and nearby structures. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division, the Ohio Attorney General’s Office Bureau of Criminal Investigation, and the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency Special Investigations Unit, conducted the investigation with support from the U.S. Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration. Related Press Release: https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/ohio-company-pleads-guilty-worker-death-case-0 United States v. Joseph Nunez, et al. No. 24-CR-00066 (District of Colorado) AUSA Jennifer Lee Springer SAUSA Linda Kato SAUSA Eric Nelson On September 9, 2026, Joseph Nunez pleaded guilty to storing hazardous waste without a permit in violation of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) (42 U.S.C. § 6928(d)(2)(A)). Co-defendants Mark Fukuzawa and Doug Watson previously pleaded guilty to the same charge. Nunez was the owner and operator of EcoGen, Inc., located in Grand Junction, Colorado. Fukuzawa was the vice-president and Watson worked as the operations manager. EcoGen, now defunct, processed hemp plants using acetone, butane, and other solvents to extract cannabidiol (CBD). This process generated many drums of ignitable waste. Between 2019 and 2020, the defendants illegally stored this waste without a hazardous waste storage permit and without labelling the 55-gallon drums, many of which were rusted and leaking. They abandoned the waste in 2020, forcing the new owners of the facility to properly dispose of more than 100 drums. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division conducted the investigation. United States v. Derek Partain, et al. No. 4:26-CR-40047 (Southern District of Illinois) ECS Senior Trial Attorney Lana Pettus AUSA Kevin Burke ECS Paralegal Chloe Harris On September 10, 2026, Derek Partain pleaded guilty to a single count of conspiracy to defraud the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) based on his conduct during and after an underground mine fire in August 2021. Partain was the second shift longwall foreman for M-Class Mining, which operated the MC #1 Mine in Franklin County, Illinois, where the fire occurred. The former manager of the mine, Brandon Parsons, also pleaded guilty to a conspiracy to defraud MSHA on August 28, 2025. Parsons’ sentencing is set for March 25, 2027, and Partain is scheduled for January 14, 2027. On August 4, 2026, prosecutors charged four defendants in a nine-count indictment relating to the 2021 fire. Those defendants are Ronald D. Koontz, the former general manager of a company providing oversight and support for M-Class and the mine; former mine Superintendent Demitrios George Macropoulos; former Second Shift Manager Randy L. Nowland; and former Third Shift Manager Cory Taylor Humphrey. On August 13, 2021, a fire ignited in the MC#1 Mine as personnel used cutting torches to cut collapsed steel beams in the mine that had blocked an entryway to the mining face and stopped the mining equipment from moving. When the fire could not be extinguished within 10 minutes, the approved Mine Emergency Evacuation and Firefighting Plan required the company to evacuate the miners and notify the U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA). The defendants decided not to follow the plan. Instead, they directed that workers continue to mine coal while others engaged in ad hoc firefighting efforts overnight and through the following morning of August 14. MSHA was ultimately alerted to the existence of the fire by an anonymous tip on the morning of August 14. After confirming the existence of the fire, MSHA issued a safety order evacuating the mine. The safety order further prohibited miners from re-entering the mine without prior notification to and authorization from MSHA. The Agency also began investigating the cause of the fire and the response of M-Class and its employees. Koontz, Macropoulos, Nowland, and Humphrey are charged with conspiring to defraud MSHA by concealing the fire and other hazards at the mine. The defendants also took steps to interfere with MSHA’s investigation of the fire and the Agency’s ability to administer safety-related orders in the aftermath of the fire. Those steps include falsifying records, not wearing tracking devices that would track and record their locations within the mine, lying to other miners about the reason for stopping work at the mine, and concealing at least one portable gas detector from MSHA inspectors. The defendants kept the miners working underground for all or portions of three shifts while unsuccessfully fighting the fire. The defendants are charged with violating a mandatory safety standard under the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act (the Mine Act) by refusing to timely evacuate the mine and failing to notify MSHA as required. Nowland and Humphrey are charged under the Mine Act with falsifying records required to document mine hazards. Koontz and Macropoulos are charged with obstructing an MSHA proceeding for entering the mine in violation of the MSHA safety order. Koontz is further charged with obstruction for directing another supervisor to delete a record reflecting a telephone call Koontz made to the supervisor after MSHA began its investigation of the fire. (18 U.S.C. §§ 371, 1505,1519; 30 U.S.C. §§ 820(c),(d)). The Department of Labor Office of Inspector General and the Federal Bureau of Investigation conducted the investigation. United States v. Michael J. Hale No. 1:26-CR-00043 (Western District of New York) AUSA Aaron Mango On September 16, 2026, Michael J. Hale pleaded guilty to making a false statement in connection with dumping hazardous waste (18 U.S.C. § 1001(a)(2)). Sentencing is scheduled for December 22, 2026. In October 2023, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) received a tip report about a large quantity of hand sanitizers dumped outside a warehouse. After executing a search warrant in December 2023, EPA investigators determined that the waste consisted of expired hand sanitizer boxes and bottles spread over an area measuring 73 feet long, 24 feet wide, and five feet high. Samples confirmed the sanitizer is an ignitable hazardous waste under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. At the time, Hale worked as the Vice President of Regional Logistics Group, LLC, a warehousing business located at 3800 Highland Avenue. When questioned, Hale denied knowing how the sanitizer appeared behind the building. Investigators already determined that the product had been delivered to the business between January and May of 2022. The U.S. Environmental Protect Agency Criminal Investigation Division and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation conducted the investigation. Photo of waste behind property included with press release Related Press Release: https://www.justice.gov/usao-wdny/pr/lockport-man-pleads-guilty-lying-about-hazardous-waste-dumped-niagara-falls Sentencings United States v. American Distillation, Inc., et al. Nos. 7:25-CR-00097, 7:24-CR-00104 (Eastern District of North Carolina) AUSA David Berak On September 4, 2026, a court sentenced American Distillation, Inc. (ADI), to complete a five-year term of probation, after pleading guilty to violating the Clean Water Act (CWA) (33 U.S.C. §§ 1311, 1319(c)(2)(A)). Company owner Andrew Simmons was sentenced in July 2026 to 10 months’ incarceration, followed by one year of supervised release, after pleading guilty to criminal tax violations (26 U.S.C. § 7203). Simmons will also pay $112,193 in restitution to the Internal Revenue Service. ADI is a chemical processing company located beside the Cape Fear River that blends and markets industrial-grade ethyl alcohol. ADI regularly receives large quantities of tert-Butyl alcohol (TBOH), which it distills into a usable product. TBOH is a highly flammable, colorless, oily liquid with a sharp alcohol odor, and is designated as a pollutant under the CWA. During distillation, ADI created and stored byproducts and wastewater, including TBOH, in a 250,000-gallon storage tank known as “Tank 14.” ADI’s National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Permit requires the company to properly dispose of TBOH byproduct. Barry Darnell White worked as a production manager for ADI. His responsibilities included overseeing the transfer of chemicals between tanks as well as monitoring the tanker trucks travelling in and out of ADI’s facilities. White reported directly to corporate management. Between 2020 and 2024, White released approximately 2,500 gallons of liquid wastewater from Tank 14, five to six times per year. White connected a hose to Tank 14, which drained into a pipe connected to an outfall flowing directly to the river. White pleaded guilty to violating the CWA and was sentenced in June 2026 to eight months of home confinement as a condition of a two-year term of probation. White also will pay a $5,000 fine. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division and the EPA Office of Inspector General conducted the investigation. United States v. Teunis Jan Willemsen No. 3:26-mj-08002 (Northern District of Ohio) AUSA Matthew Simko On September 8, 2026, a court sentenced Teunis Jan Willemsen to pay a $25,000 fine, serve 15 months of probation, and perform 100 hours of community service. Willemsen pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Water Act for negligently discharging a pollutant (33 U.S.C. §§ 1311(a), 1319(c)(1)(A)). Willemsen worked as the manager for Heartland Dairy in Rockland, Ohio. On December 12, 2022, the dairy illegally discharged wastewater into the Little Black Creek, a tributary of Saint Mary's River, causing a significant fish kill. Environmental officials responded and questioned Willemsen. Willemsen stated he was responsible for employees pumping the contents from the settling basin into a nearby drainage ditch. The discharge, consisting of manure and silage leachate, included concentrated amounts of ammonia. Heartland Dairy did not have a permit to discharge any pollutant. The Ohio Department of Agriculture determined that the discharge killed approximately 789 fish and 1,370 other animals. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division and the Ohio Department of Agriculture conducted the investigation. Press Release: https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndoh/pr/dairy-manager-sentenced-role-polluting-waterway-waste-caused-fish-kill United States v. Thao Duong, United States v. Lam Mai Nos. 3:25-CR-000511, 00512 (Northern District of Texas) ECS Trial Attorney Lauren Steele AUSA Vincent J. Mazzurco ECS Paralegal Chloe Harris On September 8, 2026, a court sentenced a wife and husband, Thao Duong and Lam Mai, for operating a website selling veterinary drugs and pesticides smuggled into the United States from Mexico. Duong will serve three months of incarceration, followed by two years of supervised release, and will forfeit more than $1.5 million. Mai was sentenced to complete a two-year term of probation. Both pleaded guilty to conspiracy (18 U.S.C. § 371). In 2011, Duong began using various online platforms to sell animal care products to customers throughout the U.S. The products she sold were used primarily by people engaged in rooster fighting ventures. Duong was not a veterinarian and did not require customers to provide veterinary prescriptions to purchase veterinary drugs. She also sold products such as Cipio Vet, Baytril Max, and Caterrol, which are produced in Mexico and not approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in the United States. In 2017, she added the pesticides Taktic and Bovitraz to her inventory. Neither Taktic nor Bovitraz are registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for sale or use and could not be sold legally in the U.S. Amitraz, the active ingredient in Taktic and Bovitraz, is toxic to bees if released into hives, and then ultimately to humans when it ends up in honey, honeycomb, and beeswax. In 2018, Duong started a website, which she used as her primary means of selling and distributing veterinary drugs and pesticides. After launching the site, Duong entered into agreements with several co-conspirators to purchase veterinary drugs and pesticides that she knew had been smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico. The smuggled pesticides and veterinary drugs came into this country through the Calexico Port of Entry in Imperial County, California, and were placed in storage units near the border. Duong’s co-conspirators then shipped the products from California to Texas. Between 2018 and 2022, Duong obtained approximately $2.4 million worth of smuggled merchandise from her co-conspirators. Mai worked as the shipping manager for the website. After orders were received, he packaged the pesticides and veterinary drugs and distributed them to customers throughout the country using the U.S. Postal Service and other shippers. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division and the FDA Office of Criminal Investigations conducted the investigation, with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. Press Release: Office of Public Affairs | Texas Couple Sentenced for Operating Website Selling Smuggled Pesticides and Veterinary Drugs | United States Department of Justice United States v. Mikhail Tsurikov, et al. Nos. 2:26-CR-00194, 00403 (Eastern District of Pennsylvania) ECS Trial Attorney Lauren Steele AUSA Angella Middleton ECS Paralegal Chloe Harris On September 10, 2026, a court sentenced Mikhail Tsurikov to complete a three-year term of probation. Tsurikov pleaded guilty to one count of violating the Act to Prevent Pollution from Ships (33 U.S.C. § 1908(a)). Tsurikov worked as the second engineer for the M/V MSC Samira III. On January 27, 2025, he caused the master of the vessel to present a false Oil Record Book (ORB) to U.S. Coast Guard inspectors during a Port State Control Examination in the Port of Philadelphia. The ORB did not contain entries for oily bilge water discharges the crew made without using a properly functioning Oil Water Separator. On August 28, 2026, MSC Shipmanagement Limited (MSC) and Hong Kong Spirit Shipping and Trading Limited pleaded guilty and were sentenced to pay a combined fine of $1.75 million and complete four-year terms of probation. The U.S. Coast Guard Sector Delaware Bay and U.S. Coast Guard Investigative Service conducted the investigation. United States v. Leshon E. Johnson No. 6:25-CR-00012 (Eastern District of Oklahoma) ECS Senior Trial Attorney Adam Cullman AUSA Jordan Howanitz ECS Paralegal Jillian Grubb ECS Law Clerk Amanda Backer On September 10, 2026, a court sentenced Leshon E. Johnson to serve 60 months’ incarceration, followed by three years of supervised release, and pay a $30,000 fine. A jury convicted Johnson in August 2025 on three counts of possession of a dog for use in an animal fighting venture and three counts of sale of a dog for use in an animal fighting venture (7 U.S.C. § 2156(b), 18 U.S.C. §§ 49, 2). Johnson ran a dog fighting operation known as “Mal Kant Kennels” in both Broken Arrow and Haskell, Oklahoma. He possessed 190 pit bull-type dogs that were seized by federal authorities in October 2024. This is believed to be the largest number of dogs ever seized from a single person in a federal dog fighting case. He previously ran “Krazyside Kennels,” also in Oklahoma, which led to his conviction on state animal fighting charges in 2004. Johnson bred “champion” and “grand champion” fighting dogs (dogs that have won three or five fights, respectively) to produce offspring with desirable fighting traits and abilities. Johnson marketed and sold stud rights and offspring from winning fighting dogs to other dog fighters looking to incorporate the Mal Kant Kennels “bloodline” into their own dog fighting operations. The Federal Bureau of Investigation conducted the investigation. Related Press Release: https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/former-nfl-player-sentenced-5-years-prison-operating-large-scale-dog-fighting-and United States v. Carl Fioravanti No. 1:23-CR-00555 (Northern District of Illinois) AUSA Tim Chapman SAUSA Samuel Cardick On September 10, 2026, a court sentenced Carl Fioravanti to 80 months of incarceration, followed by two years of supervised release. Fioravanti pleaded guilty to wire fraud and filing a false tax return for leaving asbestos at a suburban Chicago demolition site after accepting full payment for the purported remediation (18 U.S.C. § 1343; 26 U.S.C. § 7206(1)). Fioravanti is the president of Alliance Environmental Control, Inc. (Alliance) a company that performs asbestos removal services. In 2023, a property owner hired Alliance to remove regulated asbestos-containing materials (RACM) before a planned demolition of a largely abandoned medical campus in Waukegan, Illinois. The site owner agreed to pay Alliance nearly $1.8 million to properly remove the RACM. During the remediation, Fioravanti fabricated air-sampling clearance reports that fraudulently stated that the site had been scientifically tested and was clear of asbestos. Two months after Fioravanti certified the project as fully remediated, the property owner learned that Alliance had left significant amounts of RACM throughout the site. To date, the site owner has spent more than $26 million to clean up the property. Fioravanti also defrauded the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the State of Illinois of more than $2.7 million in combined tax revenues. He caused a tax preparer to file false individual and corporate income tax returns that greatly understated the amount of income Alliance and Fioravanti had earned for the years 2013 through 2022. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Housing and Urban Development Office of Inspector General, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation conducted the investigation with assistance from the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. Press Release: Northern District of Illinois | President of Environmental Company Sentenced to More Than Six and a Half Years in Prison for Leaving Asbestos at Suburban Chicago Demolition Site | United States Department of Justice United States v. Caleb Warren Randall, et al. No. 3:25-CR-00196 (Middle District of Tennessee) ECS Trial Attorney Rachel Roberts AUSA Ahmed A. Safeeullah ECS Paralegal Chloe Harris On September 11, 2026, a court sentenced Caleb Warren Randall to complete a two-year term of probation. Randall pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (18 U.S.C. § 371); Co-defendant David Ray Stark pleaded guilty to conspiring to violate the Clean Water Act for bypassing treatment processes and tampering with a monitoring device at the facility (18 U.S.C. § 371). Stark is set for sentencing on December 6, 2026. Randall and Stark managed a Nashville waste treatment facility. Stark worked as the facility operations manager and Randall was the plant supervisor at a facility operated by Allwaste Onsite, doing business as Onsite Environmental (Onsite). As part of the conspiracy, Stark and Randall directed Onsite employees to discharge untreated and partially treated wastewater into the Nashville sewer system in December 2022 and January 2023. Stark and Randall also tampered with and caused Onsite employees to tamper with a sampling device that the Nashville Metro Water Services (MWS) had installed to monitor Onsite’s compliance with its pretreatment permit. In December 2025, Onsite was sentenced to pay a $512,000 fine, representing $16,000 per day of bypassing, and complete a three-year term of probation. As a special condition of probation, Onsite must comply with a consent order previously issued by a state court, which Onsite entered into with MWS to enact a facility operating plan. Additionally, as part of the consent order, Onsite paid $86,628 to MWS for expenses related to sewer repairs and clean-up, $299,576 for surcharges related to pollutant exceedances, and $50,387 for water and sewer charges. The company will also implement several plant and equipment upgrades. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division and EPA Office of Inspector General conducted the investigation. United States v. Alfredo Vela, et al. No. 5:25-CR-01100 (Southern District of Texas) AUSA Michael T. Poyfair On September 11, 2026, a court sentenced Alfredo Vela to serve 18 months’ incarceration, followed by one year of supervised release and perform 40 hours of community service. Vela pleaded guilty to conspiracy and smuggling (18 U.S.C. §§ 371, 545). Co-defendant Janely Aylin Vela pleaded guilty to violating the Lacey Act for attempting to illegally import two Capuchin monkeys into the United States (16 U.S.C. §§ 3372(a)(2), 3373(d)(1)(A)). On June 9, 2025, a county deputy stopped Janely Vela’s car on an interstate in La Salle County, Texas. During the traffic stop, the deputy noted a covered item in the rear seat. When he asked what was in the back, she answered “her monkeys.” Further investigation determined that the monkeys were Capuchin monkeys and that Janely Vela did not have the proper licenses to possess them. Upon further questioning, Janely Vela admitted she planned to smuggle the two monkeys for Alfredo Vela, her co-conspirator. She took the animals from Nuevo Laredo, Mexico, and would have earned $500 to transport them to San Antonio, Texas. Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation. title: Former Missouri Middle School Principal Indicted on Child Pornography Charge
body: Press Release Former Missouri Middle School Principal Indicted on Child Pornography Charge Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Missouri ST. LOUIS – The former assistant principal of a Missouri middle school appeared in court this week to answer a child pornography charge. Daniel Ott, 41, was indicted in U.S. District Court in St. Louis on October 14 with one count of receiving child pornography. Juan C. Valencia, 43, was indicted the same day with one count of distribution of child pornography. Ott appeared in court and pleaded not guilty Monday. Valencia appeared in court and pleaded not guilty Thursday. The indictment accuses Ott of receiving files containing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) between Sept. 1, 2024, and Sept. 3, 2026. Valencia’s indictment accuses him of distributing CSAM, including the same two files, during the same period. A motion seeking to have Ott held in jail until trial says that he engaged in numerous conversations on Telegram during which he spoke about his attraction to minor girls, including some of the female students who attended his school. A motion seeking to hold Valencia in jail says he distributed CSAM to a middle school principal via Telegram. Both charges carry a potential penalty of five to 20 years in prison. Charges set forth in an indictment are merely accusations and do not constitute proof of guilt.  Every defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations and St. Charles County Cyber Crime Task Force investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sila Karacal is prosecuting the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Department of Justice Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc . Contact Robert Patrick, Public Affairs Officer, robert.patrick@usdoj.gov. Updated October 22, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Components Office of Foreign Litigation USAO - Missouri, Eastern

title: Illegal Alien Arrested for Identity Theft and Federal Assistance Benefit Fraud
body: Press Release Illegal Alien Arrested for Identity Theft and Federal Assistance Benefit Fraud Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts Defendant allegedly used stolen identity to receive over $11,000 in SNAP benefits BOSTON – A Dominican national unlawfully residing in Dorchester, Mass. has been arrested and charged for allegedly using a stolen identity to fraudulently obtain Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, previously known as food stamps. Juana Milagros Peña Peña, 37, was charged by criminal complaint with one count each of theft of government money, aggravated identity theft and SNAP fraud. Peña was arrested at her home on Oct. 19, 2026 and released on conditions following an initial appearance in federal court in Boston. According to the criminal complaint, Peña – a citizen of the Dominican Republic, who has been unlawfully residing in the United States since at least 2016 – fraudulently used the identity of a U.S. citizen to apply for and receive over $11,000 in SNAP benefits dating back to 2021. The victim, whose birth certificate and Social Security number Peña has fraudulently passed off as her own, reported to authorities that the theft of her identity has negatively affected her credit and has required her to utilize a special PIN when filing her taxes. The charge of SNAP fraud provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of theft of government money provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of aggravated identity theft provides for a mandatory two-year prison sentence to run consecutively to any other sentence imposed, one year of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed.  Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes that govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement. Valuable assistance was provided by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Office of Inspector General; the Social Security Administration, Office of the Inspector General; and the Massachusetts State Police. Assistant U.S. Attorney John Potapchuk of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. On March 26, 2026 , United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced the creation of the Benefit & Voter Fraud Team, a district-wide initiative established in response to the rampant fraud being uncovered across Massachusetts. Members of the public are encouraged to report suspected benefit fraud in Massachusetts by calling 1-855-SCAM-MA-1 (855-722-6621). On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law. Updated October 22, 2026 Topics Fraud Benefit Fraud Identity Theft Immigration Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: Frankfort Man Sentenced for Armed Methamphetamine Trafficking
body: Press Release Frankfort Man Sentenced for Armed Methamphetamine Trafficking Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Kentucky LEXINGTON, Ky. – A Frankfort, Ky., man, Zachery Ashburn, 33, was sentenced today to 15 years of imprisonment by U.S. District Judge Robert Wier for possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of methamphetamine and possession of a firearm in furtherance of drug trafficking. On February 23, 2025, during a traffic stop in Scott County, Ashburn possessed approximately four pounds of methamphetamine and four firearms. The methamphetamine was packaged in two separate vacuum-sealed packages that he admitted that he intended to distribute to others. Additionally, Ashburn possessed the firearms to provide protection while he was transporting the methamphetamine. Jason Parman, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Kentucky; Olivia Olson, Special Agent in Charge, FBI, Louisville Field Office; and Chief Darin Allgood, Georgetown Police Department, jointly announced the sentence. The investigation was conducted by the FBI and Georgetown Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Emily Greenfield prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States. – END – Contact CONTACT:  Jenny Parker PHONE:  (859) 685-4906 E-MAIL: jenny.parker@usdoj.gov Updated October 22, 2026 Topic Drug Trafficking Component USAO - Kentucky, Eastern

title: Two Felons Sentenced for Illegal Possession of Firearms Following Investigation Prompted by YouTube and Instagram Videos
body: Press Release Two Felons Sentenced for Illegal Possession of Firearms Following Investigation Prompted by YouTube and Instagram Videos Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia WASHINGTON – Travis Foster, 25, and Reginald Monroe, 23, both previously convicted felons residing in the District of Columbia, were sentenced today in U.S. District Court for unlawfully possessing firearms that authorities recovered following an investigation prompted by videos and livestreams posted to YouTube and Instagram, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. “They flaunted guns for the cameras, brandished weapons in music videos, and carried an arsenal of deadly firepower into our community,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Now they’re going to prison. Let this be a warning: if you are a convicted felon who continues to arm yourself and put the public at risk, you will face prison time.” Foster pleaded guilty on July 24 before U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan to unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon and unlawful possession with intent to distribute marijuana. In addition to the 57‑month prison term, Judge AliKhan ordered Foster to serve three years of supervised release. Monroe pleaded guilty on July 23 before Judge AliKhan to unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon and unlawful possession of a machine gun. In addition to the 46‑month prison term, Judge AliKhan ordered Monroe to serve three years of supervised release. A frame grab from a video posted by a co-defendant to social media. YouTube videos and Instagram live streams prompted the investigation. Investigators recognized the displayed weapons as real firearms. According to court documents, law enforcement began monitoring social media in 2023 after observing Foster and associates appearing in high‑resolution music videos and online posts with firearms equipped with extended magazines. Investigators recognized the displayed weapons as real firearms and noted the presence of micro draco pistols capable of firing rifle rounds, dramatically increasing the risk posed to the public by the firearms. According to court documents, on Oct. 19, 2023, officers tracked Foster, Monroe and others from a dinner gathering to a nightclub in NW Washington. Surveillance ultimately led law enforcement to a nearby parking garage, where officers recovered 842 suspected fentanyl pills and multiple firearms from a stolen Audi Q7, along with six more firearms from a Chrysler 300. Prescription paperwork inside a backpack found in the Chrysler 300 tied Foster to some of the recovered guns. Monroe was captured on surveillance footage exiting the Chrysler, and DNA evidence later linked him to a Glock 23 .40 caliber pistol recovered from the Audi and a Glock 32 .357 caliber pistol recovered from the Chrysler 300. Investigators later recovered Instagram voice messages in which Foster referred to the recovered firearms as his and discussed replacing them after the seizure. Additional posts showed Foster marketing marijuana for sale and possessing distribution level quantities. Law enforcement later executed a search warrant at Foster’s residence where they recovered a loaded pistol with an extended magazine, more than one pound of marijuana, and a money counter. According to court documents, Monroe’s possession of firearms was part of a longer pattern of armed criminal conduct, including prior convictions for armed robbery and unlawful firearm possession. He possessed two pistols modified to function as machine guns, each equipped with a 22‑round magazine. These weapons were carried while Monroe traveled with associates who had an arsenal of additional firearms, including micro draco pistols capable of firing rifle rounds. This case marks Foster’s second conviction involving the illegal possession of a firearm. Foster previously pleaded guilty to an October 2019 armed robbery of a car was sentenced to 96 months imprisonment. Three months after he was released on July 14, 2023, he committed the instant offense. Monroe’s conviction in this case marks his fourth for illegally possessing a firearm in just six years. Monroe also is awaiting sentencing in a Superior Court case in connection with an armed robbery. The investigation was conducted by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Washington Field Office; the FBI Washington Field Office; and the Metropolitan Police Department. The matter was prosecuted under the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful initiative by Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Helfand. Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful is a law enforcement initiative in support of President Trump's Executive Order to crack down on gun violence, prioritize federal firearms violations, pursue tougher penalties, and seek detention for federal firearms violators. 24cr1053 Law enforcement recovered two Romarm/Cugir Micro Draco AR-style pistols from the backpack containing Travis Foster’s prescription paperwork. title: New Orleans Man Indicted for Violating the Federal Controlled Substances Act
body: Press Release New Orleans Man Indicted for Violating the Federal Controlled Substances Act Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS, LA – On October 16, 2026, HAROLD BANKS ("BANKS"), age 48, of New Orleans, was indicted on two counts of distribution of controlled substances, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(B), and 841(b)(1)(C), announced United States Attorney David I. Courcelle. According to court records, Count One alleges that on August 17, 2026, BANKS did knowingly and intentionally distribute a quantity of a mixture and substance containing a detectable amount of cocaine base, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 841(a)(1) and (b)(1)(C). Count Two alleges that on September 21, 2026, BANKS did knowingly and intentionally distribute twenty-eight grams or more of a mixture and substance containing a detectable amount of cocaine base, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 841(a)(1) and (b)(1)(B). If convicted of Count One, BANKS faces up to twenty (20) years of imprisonment, up to a $1,000,000 fine, at least three (3) years of supervised release, and a $100 mandatory special assessment fee. If convicted of Count Two, BANKS faces a mandatory minimum of five (5) years up to forty (40) years of imprisonment, up to a $5,000,000 fine, at least four (4) years of supervised release, and a $100 mandatory special assessment fee. U.S. Attorney Courcelle reiterated that the indictment is merely a charge and that the guilt of the defendant must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.  It is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Troy L. Bell of the Violent Crime Unit. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. *        *        * Contact Shane M. title: Oklahoma Man Guilty of Conspiracy, False Distress Signals, and False Statements
body: Press Release Oklahoma Man Guilty of Conspiracy, False Distress Signals, and False Statements Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS , LOUISIANA – MELVIN EMDE ("EMDE") , age 44, resident of LeFlore County, Oklahoma, pled guilty on October 14, 2026, to conspiracy to commit a federal offense against or defraud the United States or an agency thereof, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 371, and communication of a false distress message to the United States Coast Guard, in violation of Title 14, United States Code, Section 521(c), announced United States Attorney David I. Courcelle. According to court documents, on or about August 7, 2023, MELVIN , and others, planned to fake MELVIN’s death to avoid prosecution in North Carolina for a pending sex crime involving a minor. They purchased fishing gear and brought kayaks to the banks of the Mississippi River in St. Charles Parish. MELVIN removed his ankle monitor from his pending case in North Carolina. A co-conspirator then made a false distress call to the U.S. Coast Guard, causing a search and rescue operation. MELVIN was later apprehended in Georgia using an alias. At sentencing, MELVIN faces maximum penalties of up to 5 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, up to 3 years of supervised release, and a mandatory special assessment fee of $100 for the conspiracy charge. For the charge of communicating a false distress message to the Coast Guard, MELVIN faces between 5 and 10 years in prison, up to 3 years of supervised release, a fine of up to $250,000, and a $100 mandatory special assessment fee. Sentencing has been scheduled for January 20, 2027. U.S. Attorney Courcelle praised the work of the United States Coast Guard – Coast Guard Investigative Service and the St. Charles Parish Sheriff’s Office in investigating this matter.  Assistant United States Attorney Spiro G. Latsis of the General Crimes Unit oversees the prosecution. *   *   * Contact Shane M. title: Uvalde Man Sentenced to 2 Years in Federal Prison for Assaulting Border Patrol Agent at Checkpoint
body: Press Release Uvalde Man Sentenced to 2 Years in Federal Prison for Assaulting Border Patrol Agent at Checkpoint Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Texas DEL RIO, Texas – A Uvalde man was sentenced to 24 months in prison for assaulting a United States Border Patrol agent, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. According to court documents, on Jan. 6, Maximiliano Arellano, 25, underwent a routine immigration checkpoint inspection at the Uvalde Border Patrol Immigration Checkpoint. Arellano was referred to a secondary inspection due to positive detection by the service canine. At secondary inspection, Arellano became agitated, repeatedly called Border Patrol agents racial slurs, and refused to comply with the agents’ commands. Arellano eventually approached an agent in an aggressive manner at which time U.S. Border Patrol agents placed Arellano against his vehicle to de-escalate the situation. Arellano resisted, pushed off of the vehicle, and threw his body into another agent. Arellano struck the agent’s chest and knocked him off balance. Arellano was ultimately restrained with the use of a taser. Arellano pleaded guilty to one count of assaulting, resisting or impeding certain officers or employees on June 30. The U.S. Border Patrol investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Carli Tuttle prosecuted the case. ### Contact USATXW.MediaInquiry@usdoj.gov Updated October 22, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - Texas, Western

title: Rapid City Woman Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison  for Her Participation in a Drug Distribution Conspiracy
body: Press Release Rapid City Woman Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison  for Her Participation in a Drug Distribution Conspiracy Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota RAPID CITY - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Court Judge Camela C. Theeler has sentenced a Rapid City, South Dakota, woman convicted of Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance.  The sentencing took place on October 20, 2026. Jaimie High Horse, 36, was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. High Horse was indicted for Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance by a federal grand jury in April 2026.  She pleaded guilty on July 21, 2026. High Horse, along with 12 co-defendants, was involved in a conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine throughout South Dakota, including Rapid City.  High Horse was personally involved in the distribution of 500 grams or more of methamphetamine.  She was arrested in April 2026 after a high-speed pursuit involving an officer with the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety. This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.  Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN).  Through PSN, the District of South Dakota seeks to bring together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce gun violence and make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. This case was investigated by the South Dakota and Colorado Drug Enforcement Administration offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Division of Drug Enforcement, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security, the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the South Dakota Highway Patrol, the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, the Rapid City Police Department, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety, the Western Colorado Drug Task Force, the Arvada, Colorado Police Department, and the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Patterson prosecuted the case. High Horse was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. Contact usasd.press@usdoj.gov Updated October 22, 2026 Topic Operation Take Back America Component USAO - South Dakota

title: Fort Bend County tax assessor-collector charged in wire fraud scheme
body: Press Release Fort Bend County tax assessor-collector charged in wire fraud scheme Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Texas HOUSTON – A federal grand jury has returned an indictment against three individuals for their alleged roles in a scheme to defraud Fort Bend County through fraudulent payroll practices. The elected tax assessor-collector of Fort Bend County—Carmen Patrice Turner, 65, Richmond—faces charges involving conspiracy, theft concerning federal program funds, and wire fraud. Also indicted are Shemerrylyn Regina Fields, 47, of Rosharon, and Victor Calvin Ewing, 69, of Houston, whom Turner allegedly hired as part of the scheme. Turner and Fields are expected to make their initial appearances before U.S. Magistrate Judge Peter Bray today in Houston. Law enforcement arrested Ewing in Chicago, Illinois, where he is expected to make his initial appearance. According to the indictment, Turner orchestrated a scheme from approximately September 2023 through September 2025 to use county payroll funds to pay individuals for work they did not perform. Turner allegedly hired Fields and another individual as deputy tax clerks but directed them to provide care for her elderly mother during regular county work hours. According to the charges, Turner instructed them to clock in and out remotely through the county’s telephone timekeeping system while falsely reporting they were performing their official duties. The indictment further alleges Turner hired Ewing as a full-time department coordinator despite knowing he already worked full-time for a company in Chicago, Illinois, and would not perform the duties of the county position. Ewing allegedly received a county salary while continuing his employment in Chicago. According to the indictment, he also agreed to transfer a portion of his county payroll deposits to Turner. In one instance, Ewing allegedly transferred money to Turner through Cash App after receiving a county payroll payment. Turner, Fields, and Ewing allegedly used false timesheets, concealed their actual work activities, and maintained access to county computer systems to create the appearance of legitimate employment. According to the indictment, Turner also used Ewing’s credentials to access WebDealer, a system county tax offices and Texas Department of Motor Vehicles use to process vehicle registrations, while Ewing was working in Chicago. The charges allege that in one of those “transactions,” Turner erroneously approved a vehicle cost of $295,836.92, instead of $29,583.92, causing the dealership a significant error in the assessed sales tax, which is automatically withdrawn from the dealership’s bank account. “Carmen Turner has been strutting around Fort Bend County with the title The Honorable for years. Nothing could be more dis- honorable—or illegal—than her and her conspirators’ public corruption,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz. “The people of the Southern District of Texas have my commitment to do everything we can to do justice and make it right. Taxpayers deserve so much better.” “Public service is a privilege, not a right to break the law,” said Special Agent in Charge Jason Hudson of FBI – Houston Field Office. “When a public official violates the law, they violate the trust of the citizens they swore to serve and protect. As a public servant myself, my hope is that today’s federal indictments and arrests are a step towards restoring that trust. If you have information about public corruption, no matter the official, the office they hold, or the loss amount, please report it.” “Through collaborative effort, justice prevails,” said Lieutenant Erik Burse of Texas Department of Public Safety. If convicted, all three face up to 20 years for each of wire fraud count. They could also receive a maximum of 10 years for theft concerning federal program funds and another five years for conspiracy. Each of the charges also carries a potential fine of up to $250,000. FBI and Texas Rangers conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Carolyn Ferko and Rodolfo Ramirez are prosecuting the case. An indictment is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law. Updated October 22, 2026 Component USAO - Texas, Southern

title: Cartel Commander Charged with International Cocaine and Methamphetamine Trafficking Conspiracy and Firearm Offenses
body: Press Release Cartel Commander Charged with International Cocaine and Methamphetamine Trafficking Conspiracy and Firearm Offenses Thursday, October 22, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs A federal grand jury in the District of Columbia returned an indictment today charging Ivan Cazarin Molina, 42, a Mexican national, with conspiracy to distribute cocaine and methamphetamine for importation into the United States and possessing a firearm in furtherance of the drug trafficking offense. According to court documents, Cazarin Molina, also known as “Tanque,” was a regional commander for the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG) in Veracruz, Mexico. On Feb. 20, 2025, the U.S. Secretary of State designated the CJNG as a foreign terrorist organization. “Today’s indictment of Ivan Cazarin Molina, a regional leader of the CJNG, sends a clear message that the Department of Justice will find all leaders and commanders of drug cartels and transnational criminal organizations and prosecute them for their destruction of our communities through drug trafficking and violence,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Today’s charges demonstrate the Justice Department’s commitment toward the total elimination of drug cartels and transnational criminal organizations. Thanks to the hard work of our DEA partners and the Criminal Division prosecutors, these cartel leaders will be exposed and their organizations dismantled.” “For two decades, Ivan Cazarin Molina allegedly helped fuel CJNG’s trafficking operations using intimidation and violence to protect its criminal enterprise,” said Administrator Terrance Cole of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). “The era of impunity for cartel leaders is over. DEA, working though the homeland security task force and alongside our international partners, will fight narco-terrorists wherever they operate – following every lead, severing every supply line, dismantling every organization, and bringing those responsible to justice.” Cazarin Molina is charged with conspiracy to manufacture and distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine and 500 grams or more of methamphetamine for importation into the United States from 2005 through 2025, and using, carrying, brandishing, and discharging a firearm, in relation to the drug trafficking conspiracy. If convicted, Cazarin Molina faces a minimum penalty of 40 years in prison and a maximum penalty of two consecutive life prison terms. Cazarin Molina was arrested on Oct. 5 by Mexican law enforcement authorities in Jalisco, Mexico. The DEA’s Special Operations Division Bilateral Investigations Unit Los Angeles is investigating the case. Chief Kaitlin Sahni of the Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit (NDDU) and Trial Attorneys Maryann McGuire, Lernik Begian, and Douglas Meisel of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF) are prosecuting the case. MNF’s mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations. MNF’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit investigates and prosecutes the top command and control elements of international drug cartels, drug trafficking organizations and related transnational criminal organizations. This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
